title: Polyester filament yarn makers (POY / FDY)
subtitle: Large continuous-process plants turning PTA and MEG into polyester yarn
covers: This page covers polyester filament yarn manufacturing (POY and FDY). It is mostly a large-company segment; banks in the region meet it as the main supplier to their MSME borrowers. Texturising (DTY) has its own page.

snapshot.text: A few large companies dominate: the top five hold over 65% of capacity, and Reliance has close to 40% of the POY market.
Reliance's list prices on 21 Nov 2026: PTA Rs 93.90/kg, MEG Rs 71/kg, polyester melt Rs 104.89/kg, all falling through November.
For a credit officer this page matters mostly as context: yarn makers' price decisions set the margins of texturisers and weavers downstream.

items.text: POY (partially oriented yarn) and FDY (fully drawn yarn) are continuous polyester filaments made by melting polymer and spinning it through fine holes. POY is mainly sold to texturisers; FDY goes straight to weavers and knitters.
The Textile Commissioner's old Surat profile counted 3 synthetic staple fibre / filament yarn manufacturing units in the cluster (data about 2004-05).

items.text: Named large producers: Reliance Industries, Indo Rama Synthetics, Century Enka, JBF Industries and Garden Silk Mills (top five, over 65% of capacity).
Sumeet Industries, a Surat-based maker, is rated by CRISIL with about 52,500 tonnes a year of POY and 45,500 tonnes a year of FDY capacity.

blocks.note: General description of a polyester filament plant. Confirm with the customer's project report.

steps.d: PTA and MEG react to form polyester melt (or chips are bought and remelted).
Melt is pushed through spinnerets into fine filaments and cooled.
Filaments are wound as POY, or drawn further to make FDY.
Denier, lustre and lot checked; packed on bobbins for dispatch.

items.text: SGCCI says the basic customs duty exemption on MEG and PTA ended on 15 Jul 2026 (chamber's statement; customs notification not checked).
BIS quality control orders on polyester fibre, polyester yarns (including POY and filament yarn), PTA and MEG were withdrawn on 12 Nov 2025; the viscose staple fibre QCO was withdrawn on 18 Nov 2025.
GST on man-made fibre was cut from 18% to 5% and on man-made yarn from 12% to 5% (GST Council, 3 Sep 2025).
Pollution category and environmental clearance for a polymer and yarn plant were not checked. Ask for the GPCB consent and any environmental clearance.
These are capital-heavy continuous plants; a stoppage is costly, so power and raw-material supply contracts matter.

Power: GERC's FY2025-26 DGVCL tariff schedule lists the Non-RGP rate (loads up to 40 kW) at 435 paise a unit up to 10 kW and 465 paise above 10 kW, plus fixed charges and 45 paise extra in peak hours. Larger loads fall in other categories. A new FY2026-27 order was issued on 25 Mar 2026, so confirm current rates from the customer's bills.

sections.title: Sales: who buys, how, and credit periods

items.text: Buyers are texturisers (POY), and weavers and knitters (FDY). Surat's cluster uses about 1.52 lakh tonnes of polyester yarn a month, about 60% as DTY.
Yarn dealers reportedly charge downstream weavers 1.5% a month on late payment, which suggests a credit chain from maker to dealer to weaver.
CRISIL on one Surat yarn maker (FY2025): debtors 31 days, inventory 39 days, gross current assets 99 days; it must give credit because its customers are small and medium players.
Credit terms of other yarn makers and dealers: not public. Collect from the customer.

sections.title: Fragility points and early warning signs for a lender

items.text: Crude oil, PTA and MEG prices move the cost base every week; the chamber says domestic prices can stay above import parity for a while.
Import policy changes (QCO removal in Nov 2025) let cheaper imported yarn compete with domestic makers.
Downstream demand stress: weavers reported running near half capacity in 2026, which cuts yarn offtake.
Cheque returns or frequent overdraws; cash credit used near the limit all month.
Electricity units falling month on month, or a shift stopped, without a matching fall in loan outstanding.
Creditor days stretching; suppliers charging late-payment interest; purchases switched to cash from new sources.
Stock or receivables building up; sales concentrated on one or two parties or brokers.
